lesson.title: Types of Business Models: Who Pays, How, and Through Which Route
lesson.summary: Companies can be grouped by who their customers are, how money comes in, how the product reaches the customer, and where they sit in the value chain. Recognising these types helps you judge how stable a firm's revenue is, how much capital it needs and what risks it carries.

sections.heading: Think of a business model as a recipe
sections.body_markdown: A **business model** is a company's recipe for creating value for customers and turning that value into profit. Two restaurants can serve the same food and still run on very different recipes: one sells meals at the counter, another sells a monthly meal subscription, and a third licenses its name to other owners. No single list covers every model, so analysts sort models using several lenses: **who the customer is**, **how revenue is earned**, **how the product is delivered**, and **the company's strategy**. One company usually fits several categories at once.

sections.heading: Lens 1: Who is the customer?
sections.body_markdown:
- **B2C (business-to-consumer):** the company sells to individuals, for example a clothing retailer or a streaming service.
- **B2B (business-to-business):** the buyer is another company, for example a firm selling machinery parts or software to manufacturers. B2B sales often involve **trade credit**, meaning the seller lets the buyer pay later, so the seller must watch customer creditworthiness and slow payers.
- **B2G (business-to-government):** the buyer is a public body, such as a contractor building a road.
- **C2C (consumer-to-consumer):** individuals sell to each other, usually through an intermediary platform such as an online auction site.

The customer type affects sales cycle length, order size, credit risk and how concentrated revenue is.

sections.heading: Lens 2: How does the money come in?
sections.body_markdown:
- **Direct sale:** the customer pays once per item or job. Revenue depends on constant new sales.
- **Subscription:** the customer pays a recurring fee for ongoing access, such as a gym membership. Revenue is more predictable, but the company must keep customers from cancelling.
- **Freemium:** a basic version is free and a premium version is paid. The free tier attracts many users, but only a fraction convert to paying.
- **Advertising-funded:** users get the service cheaply or free while advertisers pay for access to their attention.
- **Razor-and-blade (bundled complements):** the core product is sold cheaply, while the profit comes from the follow-on items that must be bought repeatedly, such as printer ink or coffee capsules. A printer maker can also sell warranties and maintenance contracts in this way.
- **Marketplace/platform:** the company brings buyers and sellers together and takes a commission or fee. Its value grows as more participants join (a *network effect*), and it usually owns little inventory itself.
- **Licensing and franchising:** the owner of valuable intangibles lets others use them for a fee (see the next section).

sections.heading: Franchising and licensing up close
sections.body_markdown:
In **licensing**, the owner (licensor) lets another party (licensee) use its intellectual property, such as a patent, trademark or special process, in return for a **royalty**, a payment tied to use or sales. **Franchising** goes further: the franchisor licenses its *whole operating system*, including brand, procedures, training and support. The franchisee runs the outlet and typically pays an upfront fee plus ongoing royalties, often a percentage of sales, and sometimes an advertising contribution.

**Why it appeals to the franchisor:** it can expand quickly using other people's capital, keeps control of the brand, and can end the agreement if things go badly.

**Why it appeals to the franchisee:** a proven model, brand recognition and support from day one.

**The catch for the franchisee:** high start-up and ongoing fees, little freedom to change how things are done, and dependence on the franchisor keeping its promises and protecting the brand.

sections.heading: Lens 3 and 4: Delivery route, value-chain position and strategy
sections.body_markdown:
**Delivery route.** A company can sell **directly** to its customers (its own stores or website) or **indirectly** through intermediaries such as distributors and retailers. It can operate from physical stores (*brick-and-mortar*), online, or both. Intermediaries add reach but take a share of the margin.

**Value-chain position.** A firm may be a producer or manufacturer, a wholesaler or distributor, or a retailer. Each stage has a different cost structure and bargaining power.

**Strategy.** Firms usually try to win by **differentiation** (a product that is distinctive enough to earn a higher price), by **low cost** (the cheapest producer), or by a mix. Many aim for both, but the two aims often conflict, so most firms end up leaning one way.

On exam questions, read the description and tag the firm on each lens. One company can be B2C, subscription-based and direct all at once.

worked_example.problem: A company sells a capsule coffee machine to households for 80, about 5 above its production cost of 75. Each capsule sells for 0.60 and costs 0.20 to make. The capsules fit only this machine, and a typical customer uses 300 capsules a year. Classify the business model on the customer, revenue and delivery lenses, and estimate the yearly profit per customer from capsules alone.
steps: Customer lens: buyers are households, so the model is B2C.
Revenue lens, machine: the machine earns only about 5 per unit (80 − 75), so it is a low-margin entry product.
Revenue lens, capsules: each capsule earns 0.60 − 0.20 = 0.40 of profit before other costs.
Yearly capsule profit per customer: 300 capsules × 0.40 = 120.
Compare: 120 per year from capsules is far larger than the 5 earned on the machine, and it recurs. This is the razor-and-blade (bundled complement) pattern.
Delivery lens: the problem does not say how the product reaches households, so it could be direct or via retailers. State what is unknown instead of guessing.
worked_example.answer: B2C razor-and-blade model; capsule profit is about 120 per customer per year, compared with about 5 on the machine.

exam_traps: Confusing franchising with licensing. A franchise licenses the whole business system (brand, procedures, training, support), while a plain licence usually covers a specific asset such as a patent, trademark or process.
Treating the types as mutually exclusive. One company can be B2C, subscription-based and direct at the same time, so read for the lens the question asks about.
Calling every online company a marketplace. A marketplace connects third-party buyers and sellers and earns fees; an online retailer that sells its own stock is just a direct B2C seller.
Mixing up freemium and free ad-funded models. In freemium the revenue comes from users who upgrade to a paid tier; in ad-funded models it comes from advertisers.

Assuming the franchisee earns the profit with no downside. The franchisee pays upfront and ongoing fees and must follow the franchisor's rules, while the franchisor earns royalties with limited capital at risk.

mcqs.stem: A company makes steel fasteners and sells them in bulk to appliance manufacturers, allowing 45 days to pay. Which description of its model by customer type is most accurate?

options.text: Business-to-consumer, because the fasteners end up in homes
options.explanation: Mistake: judging by where the product ends up instead of who buys it. The buyers are manufacturers, not households.

options.text: Business-to-business, selling to companies on credit terms
options.explanation: Correct. The customers are other firms, and extending payment time is trade credit, typical of B2B sales.

options.text: Consumer-to-consumer, because many parties are involved
options.explanation: Mistake: C2C means individuals trade with each other, usually via a platform. Here a company sells to companies.

mcqs.stem: A firm sells a basic electric shaver at a thin margin but earns most of its profit from proprietary replacement heads that customers must buy every few months. This is best described as a:

options.text: razor-and-blade model that profits from repeat complementary purchases
options.explanation: Correct. The core item is cheap and the profit comes from the follow-on consumables that only fit that item.

options.text: freemium model that offers a free basic tier
options.explanation: Mistake: freemium gives away a basic version and converts some users to paid. The shaver is sold, not given away.

options.text: franchising model that licenses a full operating system
options.explanation: Mistake: franchising involves granting others the right to run the business under the brand, which is not happening here.

mcqs.stem: Which statement correctly distinguishes franchising from a simple licensing agreement?

options.text: Only franchising involves the payment of royalties to the owner
options.explanation: Mistake: royalties are the usual payment in both arrangements, so this does not separate them.

options.text: Only licensing lets the owner end the agreement if results disappoint
options.explanation: Mistake: the owner can typically end either kind of agreement. This is not the distinguishing feature.

options.text: Franchising licenses the whole operating system, not just an asset
options.explanation: Correct. A franchise bundles the brand, procedures, training and support, while a simple licence may cover only a patent, trademark or process.

mcqs.stem: A video-hosting site lets anyone watch basic content free and charges a monthly fee for an ad-free, higher-quality version. Revenue relies on a small share of free users upgrading. This is best described as:

options.text: an advertising-funded model, because users pay nothing
options.explanation: Mistake: the revenue here comes from users who upgrade, not from advertisers, even though the basic tier is free.

options.text: a freemium model with revenue from paying upgraders
options.explanation: Correct. A free basic tier draws a large user base, and a fraction converts to a paid premium tier.

options.text: a razor-and-blade model with a cheap core product
options.explanation: Mistake: razor-and-blade requires repeat purchases of complementary consumables, and here no such items are sold.

mcqs.stem: An online platform lists rooms owned by private hosts, holds no property of its own, and keeps a percentage of each booking as its fee. Which feature most clearly marks this as a marketplace model?

options.text: It sells a recurring subscription to travellers
options.explanation: Mistake: a subscription means customers pay a regular fee for ongoing access, whereas this firm earns per-booking commissions.

options.text: It owns the rooms and sets all prices itself
options.explanation: Mistake: that describes a direct seller. A marketplace connects third-party sellers and buyers instead of owning the inventory.

options.text: It earns commissions by connecting independent buyers and sellers
options.explanation: Correct. The firm owns no inventory and takes a fee from matching two sides, so its value grows as more participants join.

mcqs.stem: From the franchisee's point of view, which is a genuine disadvantage of buying into an established franchise system?

options.text: It must build its own brand reputation from scratch
options.explanation: Mistake: this is a feature of starting an independent business. A franchisee benefits from an existing, recognised brand.

options.text: It must follow the franchisor's rules and pay ongoing fees
options.explanation: Correct. Royalties, advertising contributions and strict standards on products, premises and sometimes prices reduce the franchisee's freedom and profit.

options.text: It receives no training or support after the opening day
options.explanation: Mistake: continuing support is normally part of the deal. The risk is that promised support may not be delivered, not that it is excluded.

mcqs.stem: A fitness chain charges members a fixed monthly fee for unlimited use of its own gyms, which it operates directly. Compared with a gym that sells single-visit passes, what is the main advantage of the chain's revenue model?

options.text: Revenue no longer depends on customers staying on
options.explanation: Mistake: subscription revenue depends heavily on retention. If members cancel, recurring revenue falls.

options.text: Revenue is guaranteed to exceed the cost of running the gyms
options.explanation: Mistake: a recurring fee does not guarantee profit. Costs and the number of members still determine profitability.

options.text: Revenue is more recurring and easier to forecast
options.explanation: Correct. Regular fees give a steadier, more predictable income stream than one-off sales, provided the firm keeps its members.

flashcards.front: What are the four common lenses for classifying business models?
flashcards.back: Who the customer is (B2C, B2B, B2G, C2C), how revenue is earned, how the product is delivered (direct or indirect, physical or online, and position in the value chain), and strategy (differentiation, low cost or both).

flashcards.front: How does franchising differ from plain licensing?
flashcards.back: Licensing grants the right to use specific intellectual property for a royalty. Franchising licenses the whole business system (brand, procedures, training, support), usually for an upfront fee plus ongoing royalties.

flashcards.front: What is a razor-and-blade business model?
flashcards.back: The core product is sold cheaply or at a thin margin, and most profit comes from complementary items bought repeatedly, such as ink, capsules or replacement heads.

flashcards.front: Freemium versus subscription: what is the key contrast?
flashcards.back: Freemium offers a free basic tier and earns only from users who upgrade. A subscription charges every customer a recurring fee for ongoing access.

flashcards.front: How does a marketplace (platform) model earn money?
flashcards.back: It connects independent buyers and sellers and takes a commission or fee, usually owning little inventory, and gains value as more participants join (network effect).
